teile.einleitung: The Paris Agreement is a treaty with which almost all the countries of the world want to act together against global warming. It was adopted in December 2015 at the climate conference in Paris. Switzerland takes part too.
wichtigste: The Paris Agreement was adopted in December 2015.
It was agreed at the UN climate conference COP21 in Paris.
Warming should stay well below 2 °C, if possible at 1.5 °C.
The comparison is with the time before industrialisation.
Every five years the countries submit new national climate targets.
Its predecessor was the Kyoto Protocol of 1997.
Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990.

abschnitte.titel: A treaty for the whole world
abschnitte.text: Greenhouse gases such as **carbon dioxide** are produced mainly when coal, oil and natural gas are burned. They hold back heat in the atmosphere, and the Earth gets warmer. In December 2015 representatives of almost all countries met at the UN climate conference **COP21** in Paris. There they agreed on a new treaty. It is the first in which all participating countries, rich and poorer, commit themselves to protecting the climate. It came into force in November 2016.

Global warming should stay **well below 2 °C**. In addition, the countries want to try to limit it to **1.5 °C**. It is measured in comparison with the **pre-industrial period**, usually the years 1850 to 1900, before factories and engines used a lot of coal and oil. Since then the Earth has already become well over 1 °C warmer. In the long term, no more greenhouse gases should be emitted than nature or technology can take back up.

The agreement does not lay down how much each country must save. Each country sets its own **national climate targets**. These must be submitted again every five years and should be more ambitious each time. The countries report regularly on what they have achieved. Richer countries should also support poorer countries with money for climate protection and for adapting to climate change.

Before the Paris Agreement there was the **Kyoto Protocol** of 1997. In it, mainly industrialised countries committed themselves to lower emissions. Under President Donald Trump the **United States** withdrew from the Paris Agreement. Under his successor Joe Biden it rejoined in 2021. After Trump returned to office, the government announced its withdrawal again in early 2025. Such decisions are judged differently in politics.

Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017, that is, it officially accepted it. It wants to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by **50 per cent** compared with 1990 by 2030. By 2050 Switzerland should reach **net zero**: then it should emit no more greenhouse gases than are removed again. This target is set out in the Climate and Innovation Act, which voters approved in June 2023.

gewusst: Almost all the countries in the world take part in the Paris Agreement.
When the agreement was adopted, there was loud cheering in the hall and many delegates hugged each other.

teile.einleitung: The Ticino is the most important river in the canton of Ticino, which is named after it. It rises near the Nufenen Pass, flows through Lake Maggiore and joins the Po in Italy.
wichtigste: The Ticino rises near the Nufenen Pass.
The canton of Ticino is named after the river.
Between Airolo and Biasca it flows through the Leventina.
It flows through Bellinzona, the capital of the canton.
It flows into Lake Maggiore between Locarno and Bellinzona.
Near Pavia it joins the Po, the longest river in Italy.

abschnitte.text: The **Ticino** rises near the **Nufenen Pass** in the north of Ticino. First it flows east through the **Bedretto Valley**. At **Airolo**, at the foot of the Gotthard, it turns south. The canton of **Ticino** bears the name of this river. In German the river is also called Tessin, just like the canton.

Between Airolo and **Biasca** the Ticino flows through the **Leventina**. This is the main valley of upper Ticino. The **Gotthard motorway** and the **Gotthard railway** also run through this long valley. In several places the river drops over steep valley steps. At Biasca the Brenno joins it from the Blenio Valley.

Further south the Ticino flows through **Bellinzona**, the **capital** of the canton of Ticino. The town lies at a narrow point in the valley. Its **three castles** once guarded the route over the Alpine passes. They are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Below Bellinzona the valley becomes wide and flat; this plain is called the Magadino Plain.

Between **Locarno** and Bellinzona the Ticino flows into **Lake Maggiore**. At **Sesto Calende** in Italy it leaves the lake again. After that it flows through the Po Valley and joins the **Po** near **Pavia**. The Po is the longest river in Italy and flows into the Adriatic Sea. In this way water from the Swiss Alps reaches the Mediterranean.

gewusst: The water of the Ticino ends up in the Adriatic, while the Rhine flows into the North Sea and the Rhône into the Mediterranean in France.
In the Bedretto Valley the Ticino is only a few kilometres away from the source areas of the Rhône and the Reuss.

teile.einleitung: Vulcano is a small volcanic island in the Mediterranean north of Sicily. It belongs to Italy and is one of the Aeolian Islands. Our word volcano comes from its name.
wichtigste: Vulcano belongs to Italy and lies north of Sicily.
The island is one of the Aeolian Islands, the largest of which is called Lipari.
It is named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.
The word volcano comes from the island’s name.
The last eruption lasted from 1888 to 1890.
Many visitors bathe in warm mud on the island.
You reach Vulcano by boat.

abschnitte.titel: The workshop of the fire god
abschnitte.text: The ancient Romans worshipped **Vulcan**, the god of fire and of blacksmiths. They believed his forge lay under the island. They thought the smoke and fire from the mountain were the fire of his forge. That is why they called the island Vulcano. Later this name gave us the word **volcano** for all fire-spitting mountains.

Vulcano is one of the **Lipari Islands**, which are also called the Aeolian Islands. They lie in the Mediterranean north of **Sicily** and belong to **Italy**. The largest island in the group is called **Lipari**. The island of Stromboli with its very active volcano also belongs to it. Vulcano is the southernmost of the islands and lies closest to Sicily.

The last eruption on Vulcano lasted from **1888 to 1890**. At that time many lumps of rock flew through the air. Since then the volcano has been quiet. But it is not extinct and is closely **monitored** by experts. Gases rise from the ground and from the large crater, the **Gran Cratere**.

In many places on Vulcano it smells of **rotten eggs**. This comes from **sulphur gases** rising from the ground. Near the harbour there is a pool of warm **mud** in which many people bathe. In the sea next to it, gas bubbles up from the bottom in some places. There is no bridge to the mainland, so you get to the island by **ferry** or hydrofoil.

gewusst: A certain type of explosive eruption is named after the island in scientific language: a Vulcanian eruption.
The Aeolian Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: A tornado is a violent whirlwind that reaches from a thundercloud to the ground as a rotating tube of air. It is often only a few hundred metres wide, but it can reach wind speeds of more than 400 kilometres per hour. This makes it one of the most destructive weather events on Earth.
wichtigste: A tornado is a rotating column of air between a thundercloud and the ground.
Tornadoes form from cumulonimbus clouds, that is, large thunderclouds.
The strength of a tornado is given on the Fujita scale.
In Tornado Alley in the USA there are especially many tornadoes.
A tornado over a lake or the sea is called a waterspout.
Tornadoes usually last only a few minutes.
Tornadoes also occur in Europe and in Switzerland, but much less often.

abschnitte.text: A tornado is a small but very violent **whirlwind**. It looks like a trunk or funnel reaching down from a dark thundercloud to the ground. You can see the funnel because water vapour condenses into droplets inside it and because dust and debris are whirled up. A tornado usually lasts only a few minutes, rarely more than an hour. In German it is also called a **Windhose**.

Tornadoes form from **cumulonimbus clouds**, that is, from huge thunderclouds. **Supercells** are especially dangerous: long-lasting thunderstorms with a rotating updraft. This needs warm, moist air near the ground, cooler air higher up and winds that change direction and strength with height. Then the air can draw together into a narrow whirl that reaches the ground. Meteorologists are still researching exactly how this happens.

Most of the world’s tornadoes occur in the USA, about 1000 to 1200 a year. Especially many occur in **Tornado Alley** in the middle of the country, for example in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas. There warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico meets dry, cool air from the north and west. That is why many houses have a storm cellar. Weather services issue tornado warnings by radio, mobile phone and sirens.

The strength of a tornado is given on the **Fujita scale**, which the Japanese-American researcher Tetsuya Theodore Fujita developed in 1971. It ranges from F0 for light damage to F5 for devastating destruction. Because wind speed can rarely be measured directly, it is estimated from the damage. Since 2007 an improved version, the Enhanced Fujita scale, has been used in the USA. Strong tornadoes can destroy houses and hurl cars through the air.

A tornado over a lake or the sea is called a **waterspout**. Water is whirled up as spray, and a tube of water droplets becomes visible. Waterspouts are usually weaker than tornadoes over land. They can occasionally be seen on Swiss lakes too, for example on Lake Constance or Lake Maggiore. If a waterspout moves onto land, it becomes a tornado.

In Europe too there are hundreds of tornadoes every year, but most are weak. In Switzerland tornadoes are rare. The strongest known Swiss tornado swept through the **Vallée de Joux** in the Vaud Jura on 19 August 1926 and destroyed houses and large areas of forest. If you see a tornado, you should immediately seek shelter in a cellar or a windowless room on the ground floor.

begriffe.erklaerung: Huge thundercloud that towers high into the sky.
Especially strong, long-lasting thunderstorm with a rotating updraft.
Scale from F0 to F5 used to give the strength of a tornado.
Tornado over a lake or the sea.

gewusst: The highest wind speed ever measured in a tornado was almost 500 kilometres per hour, measured by radar in Oklahoma in 1999.
In the northern hemisphere tornadoes usually turn anticlockwise.
A tornado can completely destroy one house and leave the house next door almost undamaged.

teile.einleitung: The greenhouse effect makes sure that the Earth is a pleasantly warm planet. Certain gases in the air hold on to heat, similar to the glass roof of a greenhouse. Because people are releasing more and more of these gases, the effect is getting stronger and the Earth is warming up.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases hold back the Earth’s heat radiation in the atmosphere.
Without the natural greenhouse effect it would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius on Earth on average.
With it the average temperature is about plus 15 degrees Celsius.
Carbon dioxide is the greenhouse gas that people release in the largest amounts.
Methane is produced, among other places, in the stomachs of cows.
The extra greenhouse effect caused by people leads to climate change.
The Paris climate agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground and the seas. The warm Earth gives off this energy again as invisible **heat radiation**. Part of it is absorbed by **greenhouse gases** in the air and radiated back towards the Earth. So more heat stays near the Earth’s surface. This is similar to a greenhouse, where it is warmer than outside, or to a blanket that keeps you warm.

The natural greenhouse effect is very important for life on Earth. Without it the average temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius, and the Earth would be an ice planet. Thanks to it, the average is about plus 15 degrees. The most important natural greenhouse gas is **water vapour**. Carbon dioxide also occurs naturally in the air, for example from volcanoes and the breathing of living things.

Since industrialisation, people have been burning large amounts of coal, oil and natural gas. This mainly produces **carbon dioxide**, CO2 for short, the greenhouse gas that people release in the largest amounts. Its share in the air has risen from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to more than 420 ppm (as of 2024). **Methane** is produced, among other places, in the stomachs of cows, in rice fields and at rubbish tips. Cutting down forests also strengthens the greenhouse effect, because trees store CO2.

The French researcher Joseph Fourier suspected as early as 1824 that the atmosphere warms the Earth. Around 1859 the Irishman John Tyndall proved in the laboratory that gases such as water vapour and CO2 absorb heat radiation. In 1896 the Swede **Svante Arrhenius** was the first to calculate that more CO2 would warm the Earth. Today thousands of researchers in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the **IPCC**, sum up what is known about the climate.

On average the Earth is clearly warmer today than before industrialisation. In Switzerland the temperature has even risen about twice as much as the global average since measurements began in 1864. The glaciers in the Alps are melting, and heatwaves and heavy rain are becoming more frequent. Sea level is rising because ice melts and warm water expands. Many animal and plant species have to move to higher or cooler areas.

In the **Paris climate agreement** of 2015, almost all countries committed to keeping warming well below 2 degrees and, if possible, limiting it to 1.5 degrees. In 2023 Swiss voters approved a law under which Switzerland should emit no more greenhouse gases on balance by 2050. This needs renewable energy such as solar, wind and hydropower. Everyone can help too, for example by cycling, using public transport, eating less meat and producing less rubbish.

begriffe.erklaerung: Gas in the air that absorbs and holds back the Earth’s heat radiation.
Gas produced when coal, oil, gas and wood are burned, CO2 for short.
Greenhouse gas that is produced, for example, when cows digest their food.
Long-term change in the climate, today above all the warming caused by people.
Parts per million, used to say how much of a gas there is in the air.

gewusst: Over a period of a hundred years, methane is about 25 to 30 times stronger per kilogram than carbon dioxide.
Venus has an extreme greenhouse effect, which is why it is more than 400 degrees hot there.
Swiss glaciers have lost more than half of their ice since 1850.

teile.einleitung: Lake Thun is a large lake on the edge of the Alps in the Bernese Oberland. It lies between the town of Thun and Interlaken, and the River Aare flows through it.
wichtigste: The Aare flows from Lake Brienz through Lake Thun and leaves it at Thun.
Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.
The lake is up to 217 m deep.
It is about 17.5 km long and up to 3.5 km wide.
Its area is just under 48 km².
On the shore stands Spiez Castle, and high above lie the St Beatus Caves.

abschnitte.titel: A lake in the Bernese Oberland
abschnitte.text: **Lake Thun** lies in the canton of Bern on the edge of the Alps. It is about **17.5 km** long and up to **3.5 km** wide. Its area is just under **48 km²**. That makes it about twelve times smaller than Lake Geneva. At its deepest point it measures around **217 m**. The lake fills a valley floor that glaciers carved out during the Ice Ages.

The **Aare** comes out of **Lake Brienz** and flows through Lake Thun. In the town of **Thun** it leaves the lake again and flows on towards Bern. Between the two lakes lies **Interlaken**. The name means **“between the lakes”**. The town lies on a plain that rivers built up with gravel.

On a peninsula on the south shore stands **Spiez Castle**. Together with its **Romanesque church** it towers over the Bay of Spiez. The view of castle, church and lake is one of the best-known views of Lake Thun. Thun itself also has a famous castle high above the old town. Other castles lie on the shore, such as Oberhofen.

High above the **north shore** lie the **St Beatus Caves**. They are named after **Saint Beatus**, who according to legend is said to have lived there. The caves stretch far into the mountain. You can visit them on secured paths. You can see stalactites and stalagmites, underground streams and waterfalls.

**Passenger boats** sail on Lake Thun, including a historic paddle steamer. Many people go sailing, swimming or on trips to the lakeside villages. Behind the lake rise mountains such as the **Niesen**, the Eiger, the Mönch and the Jungfrau. That is why the area is popular with tourists from all over the world.

gewusst: The Niesen on Lake Thun has an almost perfect pyramid shape and is therefore also called the Swiss pyramid.
After the last Ice Age, Lake Thun and Lake Brienz were once a single large lake.

teile.einleitung: Greenhouse gases are gases in the air that hold back heat radiation. Without them the Earth would be much colder, but the extra greenhouse gases released by people are warming the climate.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases hold back heat radiation in the atmosphere.
Carbon dioxide contributes most to the man-made greenhouse effect.
A CO2 molecule is made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Joseph Fourier described the effect around 1824, and Svante Arrhenius calculated it in 1896.
Global warming potential compares the effect of a gas with CO2.
Nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms the Earth’s surface. The surface gives off heat as **infrared radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** absorb this **heat radiation** and radiate part of it back towards the Earth. This keeps the surface warmer. The main components of air, **nitrogen** and **oxygen**, make up around 99 per cent of dry air. Their molecules, made of two identical atoms, hardly absorb heat radiation at all.

The most important greenhouse gas released by people is **carbon dioxide** (CO2). A molecule consists of one **carbon atom** and two **oxygen atoms**. It is straight, but it can vibrate and absorb heat radiation as it does so. CO2 is mainly produced by burning **coal, oil and natural gas**. It is responsible for most of the extra warming.

Other gases warm the climate too. **Nitrous oxide** (N2O) is commonly called **laughing gas**, because it used to be used as an anaesthetic. It comes mainly from **nitrogen fertiliser** in farming. The artificial gas **sulphur hexafluoride** (SF6) insulates well against electrical voltage and is used in switchgear. Per kilogram it is more than 20,000 times stronger than CO2 and stays in the air for thousands of years.

To compare gases there is the **global warming potential**. It shows how strongly a gas warms over a period, usually **100 years**, compared with the same amount of CO2. CO2 has the value **1**. Gases with a high value matter even in small amounts. Switzerland also calculates its climate targets with such values.

Around **1824** the French mathematician **Joseph Fourier** noticed that, given its distance from the Sun, the Earth should actually be colder. He suspected that the layer of air holds back heat, similar to a **glass bell jar**. In **1896** the Swedish researcher **Svante Arrhenius** was the first to calculate how much the Earth would warm with more CO2. He is regarded as a pioneer of climate research.

gewusst: Without natural greenhouse gases the average temperature of the Earth would be far below freezing.
Water vapour is also an important natural greenhouse gas.

teile.einleitung: A U-shaped valley, or glacial trough, is a valley with a U-shaped cross-section that a glacier has carved out. There are many U-shaped valleys in the Swiss Alps; the best known is the Lauterbrunnen Valley.
wichtigste: A U-shaped valley has a U-shaped cross-section, a river valley a V-shaped one.
The Lauterbrunnen Valley is a well-known U-shaped valley in the Bernese Oberland.
Side valleys that end high above the valley floor are called hanging valleys.
The flat ledge above the steep walls is called the trough shoulder.
A U-shaped valley flooded by the sea is called a fjord.
A rock barrier across the valley is called a rock bar.

abschnitte.text: A river cuts downwards and forms steep slopes that meet at the bottom. This creates a **V-shaped valley** with a **V-shaped** cross-section. A **glacier**, on the other hand, fills the whole valley. It grinds away the slopes and the floor and forms a wide **U**. Such a valley is called a **U-shaped valley**. During the Ice Ages the Alpine valleys were filled with huge glaciers.

A well-known example is the **Lauterbrunnen Valley** in the Bernese Oberland. It has a flat valley floor and almost vertical rock walls. Above the walls lies a flatter ledge, the **trough shoulder**. There you find Alpine pastures and villages such as **Mürren** and **Wengen**. The flat valley floor formed because streams and lakes deposited a lot of **gravel and sand** after the glacier retreated.

The large main glacier carved its valley much deeper than the small side glaciers. That is why the side valleys end high up in the rock wall. They are called **hanging valleys**. Their streams plunge as **waterfalls** over the steep trough wall into the main valley. A well-known example is the **Staubbach Falls** near Lauterbrunnen.

Not all rock is equally hard. A glacier grinds hard rock away less strongly. So **rock barriers** are left standing across the valley. They are called **rock bars**. Rivers have often cut through such bars in narrow gorges. After the Ice Age there was sometimes a lake behind a rock bar.

After the Ice Age the **sea level** rose because a lot of ice melted. On some coasts the sea pushed into deep glacial valleys. A U-shaped valley flooded by the sea is called a **fjord**. The fjords in **Norway** are especially famous. They are often very deep and surrounded by steep rock walls.

gewusst: In the Lauterbrunnen Valley there are a great many waterfalls that plunge down from hanging valleys.
The Reuss Valley in Uri and the Hasli Valley are also U-shaped valleys formed by glaciers.

teile.einleitung: A volcano is a mountain or an opening in the Earth’s surface from which hot, liquid rock, ash and gases come out. Volcanoes show us how hot it is deep inside the Earth. Some have been sleeping for thousands of years, others erupt almost every day.
wichtigste: A volcano forms where molten rock from inside the Earth reaches the surface.
The hot, liquid rock that flows out of a volcano is called lava.
The opening at the top of a volcano is called a crater.
When a volcano throws out lava and ash, this is called an eruption.
Etna on the Italian island of Sicily is a famous, very active volcano.
Today there are no active volcanoes in Switzerland.
Worldwide there are around 1350 volcanoes on land that are considered possibly active.

abschnitte.text: A volcano is a place where **magma** from inside the Earth pushes up to the surface. Beneath the volcano there is often a **magma chamber** in which the molten rock collects. It rises through a vent and comes out at the top in the **crater**. As soon as it is at the surface, the molten rock is called lava. Over time lava and ash pile up into a mountain.

Depending on its type, **lava** is about 700 to 1200 degrees Celsius hot. Runny lava flows down the slope like a glowing river. Thick, sticky lava, on the other hand, builds up and can lead to violent explosions. The volcano then hurls ash, lumps of rock and gases high into the air. Cooled lava becomes solid rock such as basalt.

Runny lava forms flat, wide **shield volcanoes**, like the volcanoes on Hawaii. Many layers of lava and ash build up steep, cone-shaped **stratovolcanoes**, such as Vesuvius near Naples or Fuji in Japan. Small hills of cinders are called cinder cones. If a volcano collapses in on itself after a huge eruption, a large basin forms, a caldera.

**Etna** on Sicily is the highest active volcano in Europe at more than 3300 metres and erupts often. On the island of Stromboli, the volcano of the same name spits small fountains of lava into the air almost all the time. In the year 79 AD Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii. In Iceland and on Hawaii you can sometimes even watch lava flows from a safe distance. The largest volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa on Hawaii.

Today there are no active volcanoes in Switzerland. But very close by, in the **Hegau** in southern Germany north of Schaffhausen, stand the remains of volcanoes that were active about 15 to 7 million years ago. There are also extinct volcanoes in the Eifel in Germany and in the Auvergne in France. The nearest active volcanoes from Switzerland are in Italy.

Experts who study volcanoes are called **volcanologists**. They measure small earthquakes, gases and the swelling of the ground to predict eruptions. Despite the danger, millions of people live near volcanoes. This is because volcanic soils are very fertile, and in Iceland volcanic geothermal heat is used for heating and to produce electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Molten rock below the Earth’s surface.
Molten rock that flows out of a volcano onto the surface.
Opening at the top of a volcano from which lava and ash come out.

gewusst: The largest known volcano in the solar system is Olympus Mons on Mars; it is about three times as high as Mount Everest.
Most of the Earth’s volcanoes lie unseen under the sea.
On Hawaii the land keeps growing a little bigger because of new lava.

teile.einleitung: Ocean trenches are long, narrow channels in the seabed and the deepest places on Earth. They form where one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.
wichtigste: Ocean trenches form at subduction zones.
The deepest point is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench at just under 11,000 m.
Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached it in 1960 in the submersible Trieste.
The Trieste is based on an invention by the Swiss Auguste Piccard.
Below about 6000 m the hadal zone begins.
At the bottom of the Mariana Trench the pressure is around 1100 bar.

abschnitte.text: The Earth’s surface is made of large **plates** that move slowly. Where an oceanic plate sinks beneath another, this is called a **subduction zone**. An **ocean trench** forms there. Nearby there are often **volcanic arcs** and strong **earthquakes**. Many ocean trenches lie around the Pacific.

The **Mariana Trench** in the western Pacific is the deepest. In its **Challenger Deep** just under **11,000 m** has been measured. The second deepest is the **Tonga Trench** north of New Zealand. Its Horizon Deep reaches just under 10,800 m. The deepest point of the Atlantic lies in the **Puerto Rico Trench** at around 8400 m. From about **6000 m** down, people speak of the **hadal zone**, named after the Greek Hades.

The Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard** developed the principle of the **bathyscaphe**, a submersible for the deep sea. The **Trieste** was built to his plans in Italy in **1953**. Later the US Navy took it over. On **23 January 1960** his son **Jacques Piccard** and **Don Walsh** dived in it to the Challenger Deep. It was the first crewed visit to the deepest point of the ocean.

On **26 March 2012** the film director **James Cameron** reached the Challenger Deep. In the submersible **Deepsea Challenger** he was the first person to dive there alone. Such dives are very rare, because the materials must withstand enormous forces.

In water the pressure increases by about **1 bar** for every **10 m** of depth. Just under 11,000 m divided by 10 m gives around **1100 bar**. That is more than a thousand times the air pressure at the sea surface. Even so, animals live down there too, for example amphipods and other small animals. It is always dark and cold.

gewusst: Mount Everest would fit into the Challenger Deep, and its summit would still be more than 2000 m below the water surface.
Before his submersibles, Auguste Piccard also rose into the stratosphere in a balloon.

teile.einleitung: A low-pressure area, or low for short, is an area with low air pressure. Lows often bring clouds, wind and rain and have a strong influence on the weather in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In the centre of a low the air rises.
Rising air cools down, and clouds form.
In the northern hemisphere the air flows anticlockwise around a low.
Lows usually move from the west, from the Atlantic, to Switzerland.
The Icelandic Low is a common low over the North Atlantic.
The Genoa low often brings a lot of precipitation to the southern side of the Alps.

abschnitte.text: In a **low-pressure area** the air flows together near the ground and then **rises**. As it rises it expands and **cools down**. The water vapour condenses into cloud droplets. That is why lows often bring lots of **clouds** and rain. With a high it is the other way round: there the air sinks, and the weather is usually fine.

The air does not flow straight into the low. The **Earth’s rotation** deflects it. In the **northern hemisphere** it therefore turns **anticlockwise** around the low. In the southern hemisphere it is the other way round. On weather maps you can recognise lows by the letter L (T in German) and by closely spaced lines of equal air pressure.

At our latitudes **westerly winds** mainly blow high up. They drive the lows from the **Atlantic** across Europe. That is why bad weather in Switzerland usually comes from the west. Around Iceland the air pressure is low on average; this is the **Icelandic Low**. Many lows that move to Europe form or grow stronger there.

When cold air flows over the Alps into the Mediterranean, a low can form in the Gulf of Genoa. It is called a **Genoa low**. It brings damp air towards the Alps. In **Ticino** it then often rains or snows heavily. Sometimes a Genoa low also moves further east and brings precipitation to the Eastern Alps.

A **cut-off low** is a detached low of very cold air at great height, about 5 to 10 kilometres above the ground. Because it is very cold up there, tall heaped clouds with showers and thunderstorms easily grow beneath it. In meteorology, a **hurricane** is a very strong **tropical low**. It forms over warm seas and has very low air pressure at its centre.

gewusst: Many lows over Europe are given names every year, similar to storms.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer, usually in hectopascals.

teile.einleitung: A fossil shows the remains or traces of living things that lived a very long time ago. Fossils reveal what the Earth and its animals and plants looked like in the past.
wichtigste: Petrified remains are also called fossils.
They form over many thousands to millions of years.
For this, the living thing is covered by layers of sand or mud.
Ammonites were sea creatures with a spiral-shaped shell.
In the canton of Jura there are thousands of fossilised dinosaur footprints.
Palaeontologists are researchers who study fossils.
Fossilised shells are found on Swiss mountains because there used to be sea there.

abschnitte.text: When an animal dies in water, it often sinks to the bottom. There it is covered by **sand or mud**. The soft parts decay, while hard parts such as bones, teeth or shells last longer. Over time minerals from the water seep in and turn the remains to stone. Sometimes only an **imprint** is left in the rock. All this takes a very, very long time.

Very well-known fossils are **ammonites**. They were sea creatures with a spiral-shaped shell that looks like a snail shell. They died out a long time ago. On Swiss mountains you can find fossilised shells and ammonites. The reason: a very long time ago there was a **sea** there. Later the seabed was folded up into mountains when the Alps formed.

Not only body parts can become fossils, but also **tracks**. In the **canton of Jura**, thousands of fossilised dinosaur footprints were found when the A16 motorway was built. They show where the animals once walked along a shallow seashore. There are such tracks in the Alps too.

**Amber** is fossilised tree resin and shimmers yellow to orange. When the resin was still sticky, small animals sometimes got stuck in it. So today insects that lived millions of years ago are found in amber. They are often so well preserved that you can see fine hairs and wings.

Researchers who study fossils are called **palaeontologists**. They carefully dig out finds, clean them and compare them with others. In this way they learn which animals and plants lived in the past and how life on Earth has changed. A famous site is **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, where many fossils of sea creatures and reptiles were found.

gewusst: Because of its fossils, Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Fossilised animal droppings are also fossils; they are called coprolites.

teile.einleitung: Peat is a brown to black soil made of dead plants that forms in bogs and moors. It grows very slowly and stores a lot of carbon.
wichtigste: Peat forms in bogs because the plants there do not rot completely.
In a wet bog there is not enough oxygen for the decomposers.
A layer of peat grows by about one millimetre a year.
In the past people cut peat and burned it for heating.
Since a popular vote in 1987, bogs and moors are protected in Switzerland.
After millions of years peat can turn into coal.

abschnitte.text: In a **bog** the ground is wet all year round. Dead plants, above all **peat mosses**, sink into the water. Because there is no **oxygen** there, decomposers cannot break them down completely. The remains build up and become **peat**. It is brown to blackish brown, and you can often still see bits of moss and plants in it.

Peat grows very slowly, about **one millimetre a year**. So one metre of peat takes around **a thousand years**. Many bogs in Switzerland started to grow after the last Ice Age. That is why a bog that is destroyed can hardly be replaced.

Peat used to be an important **fuel**. People cut it out of the bog with spades in brick-shaped pieces. This is called **peat cutting**. Then they dried the pieces and burned them in the stove. Especially at times when there was little wood and coal, for example during the World Wars, a lot of peat was dug in Switzerland too.

Bogs are home to many **rare animals and plants** and store a lot of **carbon**. When peat is dug, this habitat is lost. In Switzerland bogs and moors have been protected since the **popular vote of 1987**. Peat may no longer be dug there. That is why you should also use **peat-free compost** in the garden, because imported peat comes from bogs in other countries.

When peat is covered by many layers of rock and pressed together, it changes. Water is squeezed out, and the share of carbon rises. After **millions of years** it can become **lignite** (brown coal) and later **hard coal**. So peat is an early stage of coal.

gewusst: The popular initiative of 1987 is also called the Rothenthurm Initiative, after a moor in the canton of Schwyz.
In bogs, wood and other remains often stay well preserved for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: A kettle hole is a hollow in the ground that formed when buried glacier ice melted. Such holes are found where glaciers retreated after the Ice Age.
wichtigste: Dead ice is ice that has broken away from the glacier and no longer moves.
Sand and gravel cover the block of ice, so it melts only slowly.
When the ice melts, the ground sinks and a kettle hole forms.
If the hole fills with groundwater, a kettle lake forms.
In northern Germany small kettle ponds are called “Sölle”.
When a kettle lake silts up, it often turns into a bog.

abschnitte.text: When a glacier retreats, large **blocks of ice** are often left behind. They are no longer connected to the glacier and no longer move. This motionless ice is called **dead ice**. Meltwater deposits **sand and gravel** over the blocks. This layer acts like insulation, so the ice melts only very slowly.

At some point the buried block of ice does melt. Then the ice is missing under the layer of earth. The ground above it **sinks**, and a **hollow** forms. This is a **kettle hole**. Most kettle holes are **roundish** and smaller than one hectare. But they can be more than ten metres deep.

If the bottom of the hole lies below the **water table**, it fills with water. This creates a small **kettle lake**. In **northern Germany** such small round ponds are called a **“Soll”**, plural **“Sölle”**. They formed after the last cold period. There are also many kettle lakes in the **Swiss Plateau** and the Alpine foothills.

Over many centuries **plant remains** collect at the bottom of a kettle lake. Reeds and mosses grow into the lake from the shore. Gradually the lake becomes overgrown. People say it **silts up**. In the end a **bog** often forms. Such bogs are valuable habitats for rare plants and animals.

gewusst: Kettle holes are traces of the Ice Age that you can still see today in the middle of meadows and forests.
Some blocks of dead ice took hundreds to thousands of years to melt completely.

teile.einleitung: The word tuff, or tuff stone, refers to two different rocks. Volcanic tuff is made of hardened volcanic ash. Calcareous tuff, on the other hand, forms when lime is deposited from spring water. Both are porous, light and easy to work.
wichtigste: Volcanic tuff is made of hardened volcanic ash and small fragments of rock.
Tuff is one of the pyroclastic rocks.
Calcareous tuff forms when lime is deposited from spring water, often around moss.
Tuff stone is light and easy to work.
In Cappadocia in Turkey there are rock towers and cave dwellings made of tuff.
Most of the moai statues on Easter Island are carved from tuff.
The early city wall of Rome was built from blocks of tuff.

abschnitte.text: In a volcanic eruption, ash and small fragments of rock are hurled into the air. They fall back down and settle in layers. When these layers harden, **volcanic tuff** forms. Such rocks are called **pyroclastic**, which means roughly “broken by fire”. They come from the volcano but are deposited like sand or mud.

**Calcareous tuff** has nothing to do with volcanoes. Lime-rich spring water gives off **carbon dioxide** in the air. As it does so, lime is deposited and coats mosses, stalks and leaves. When the plant parts later rot away, small holes and tubes are left behind. That is why calcareous tuff often looks like a sponge made of stone.

Tuff is **porous**, light and usually quite soft. You can saw and carve it with simple tools. It also keeps out heat and cold well. That is why people built with tuff stone early on. Rome lies in an area with old volcanoes, and the **Servian Wall** was built from large blocks of tuff. In Switzerland too you can find calcareous tuff in old churches and houses.

In **Cappadocia** in Turkey, wind and water have shaped the soft tuff into rock towers. People hollowed out homes, churches and even whole underground cities in them. On **Easter Island** in the Pacific, the inhabitants carved most of their large **moai statues** from tuff in the Rano Raraku quarry. The rock was easy to work with stone tools.

gewusst: Some rock towers in Cappadocia wear a hat of harder rock on top that protects the soft tuff below.
Calcareous tuff can still grow at springs today; sometimes you can see it at waterfalls with moss.

teile.einleitung: In August 2005 it rained very heavily in Switzerland for several days. Streams and rivers burst their banks, lakes rose and debris flows destroyed houses. The flooding caused the greatest total damage since systematic records began.
wichtigste: The main cause was heavy rain lasting several days on the northern side of the Alps.
Six people died in Switzerland.
According to the Federal Office for the Environment, the damage came to around 3 billion francs.
In Bern the Matte district on the Aare was under water.
In Brienz debris flows from the Glyssibach destroyed several houses.
For days Engelberg could only be reached by air.
Afterwards a relief tunnel for Lake Thun was built in Thun.

abschnitte.text: In August 2005 a **low-pressure area** sat over Central Europe in such a way that damp air flowed again and again towards the Alps. On the **northern side of the Alps** very large amounts of rain fell over several days. The ground could no longer soak up the water. Streams and rivers swelled and burst their banks. Many lakes also rose sharply.

In the city of **Bern** the Aare flooded the **Matte** district below the old town. Further upstream the Aare burst its banks in the Belpmoos and put **Bern-Belp** airport under water. In **Brienz** on Lake Brienz, huge **debris flows** from the Glyssibach broke into the village. A debris flow is a fast stream of water, mud and stones.

In the canton of Obwalden the **Engelberger Aa** destroyed the road and railway line into the valley. So for days the monastery and holiday village of **Engelberg** could only be reached by helicopter. Other valleys were cut off too. Many people had to leave their homes and were taken to safety. The fire brigade, civil protection and the army helped with rescue and clearing up.

According to the **Federal Office for the Environment**, six people died in Switzerland. The damage to houses, roads, railway lines and fields came to around **3 billion francs**. That was the greatest total damage since systematic records began in 1972. Insurance companies paid for much of the damage, but the Confederation, cantons and municipalities also had to spend a lot of money.

After 2005 Switzerland improved its **flood protection**. Dams were built, rivers were given more space and hazard maps were drawn up. In **Thun** a **flood relief tunnel** was built. During floods it carries extra water from Lake Thun into the Aare so that the lake level falls more quickly. Warnings of severe weather were also improved.

gewusst: A debris flow can carry away large boulders that are heavier than a lorry.
Today hazard maps show for many municipalities where floods or debris flows are a threat.

teile.einleitung: Weathering is the slow breakdown of rock where it is. Weather, water and living things loosen and break down the rock. Only after that can erosion carry the particles away.
wichtigste: During weathering the rock first stays in the same place.
Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces, erosion carries it away.
There is physical, chemical and biological weathering.
When rainwater dissolves limestone, this is called chemical weathering.
Roots that push rocks apart are called root wedging.
Chemical weathering is strongest in the hot, humid tropics.
Karren are grooves that rainwater dissolves in limestone rock.

abschnitte.text: **Weathering** prepares the rock: it loosens it, makes cracks and breaks it into smaller pieces. These pieces stay where they are at first. Only during **erosion** do water, ice or wind carry the particles away. Both processes work together and shape mountains and valleys over a long time. Weathered rock also forms the **soil** in which plants grow.

In physical weathering, rock breaks without its substances changing. In **deserts** the rock gets very hot during the day and cools down sharply at night. The constant expanding and contracting causes cracks. This is called **thermal weathering**. In **salt weathering**, salty water seeps into pores and evaporates. The growing salt crystals push the rock apart. In the mountains, water freezing in cracks also splits the rocks.

Rainwater contains some **carbonic acid**, which can dissolve limestone. Because the substances change in the process, this is called **chemical weathering**. Such processes happen faster when it is warm and need water. That is why rock breaks down especially deeply in the **hot, humid tropics**. In cold or dry areas chemical weathering is weaker.

Living things also weather rock. Plant roots grow into fine cracks and get thicker. With great force they widen the gaps until the rock breaks. This is called **root wedging**. Lichens and mosses also give off substances that slowly attack the rock.

On bare limestone surfaces, rainwater dissolves grooves from very fine to a metre deep. These grooves are called **karren** or, in Swiss German, **Schratten**. When there are many side by side, this is called a **karren field** or limestone pavement. Well-known examples are on the **Schrattenfluh** in the canton of Lucerne, which is named after the Schratten, and in the **Silberen** area in the canton of Schwyz.

gewusst: The Schrattenfluh gets its name from the Schratten, the grooves in the limestone.
Water expands by about a tenth when it freezes, and that can split rocks.

teile.einleitung: A tsunami is a series of huge sea waves, usually set off by an undersea earthquake. On the open sea it is hardly noticeable, but at the coast it can grow into an enormous wall of water. Tsunamis are among the most dangerous natural disasters.
wichtigste: The Japanese word tsunami means harbour wave.
A tsunami is most often set off by an undersea earthquake.
In the deep ocean a tsunami can travel about as fast as an aeroplane.
One warning sign is when the sea suddenly draws back a long way.
On 26 December 2004 a devastating tsunami occurred in the Indian Ocean.
Tsunamis can also happen on lakes, for example in 563 on Lake Geneva.
When there is a tsunami warning, you must flee to higher ground at once.

abschnitte.text: The word **tsunami** comes from Japanese and means harbour wave. In the past, fishermen came back to a destroyed harbour even though they had noticed nothing on the open sea. Unlike normal waves made by the wind, a tsunami moves the water from the seabed to the surface. It usually consists of several waves that arrive minutes to an hour apart. The first wave is not always the biggest.

A tsunami is most often set off by an **undersea earthquake**. The seabed suddenly lifts or drops, often at a subduction zone, where one plate sinks beneath another. The whole column of water above moves with it and spreads out as a wave. Volcanic eruptions, rockfalls and underwater landslides can also set off tsunamis. Very rarely, the impact of a meteorite can be the cause.

In the deep ocean a tsunami races along at 700 to 800 kilometres per hour, about as fast as an aeroplane. There the wave is often less than a metre high, and ships hardly feel anything. Only when the water becomes shallower near the coast does the wave slow down and pile up, sometimes to more than ten metres. Often the sea suddenly draws back a long way beforehand and the seabed is exposed. This **warning sign** means: get away from the beach at once and up to higher ground!

On 26 December 2004 a huge undersea earthquake with a magnitude of about 9.1 shook the seabed off the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It set off a tsunami that hit the coasts of many countries around the **Indian Ocean**, including Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India and Thailand. More than 200,000 people died, among them tourists from Switzerland. In 2011 a tsunami devastated the east coast of Japan and led to the accident at the Fukushima nuclear power station.

Tsunamis can also form on lakes. In the year 563 a mountain collapsed in the Rhône Valley near the fortress of Tauredunum, and the debris set off a huge flood wave on **Lake Geneva**. It flooded the shores and caused great damage even in Geneva. The earthquake of 1601 in Central Switzerland also set off large waves on **Lake Lucerne**. Today researchers study the deposits on the lake bed to assess such dangers better.

After 2004 a **tsunami early warning system** was also set up in the Indian Ocean, as had long existed in the Pacific. Measuring buoys and pressure sensors on the seabed detect unusual waves. Because earthquake waves are much faster than the tsunami, there is often some time for a warning. On coasts at risk, signs show the escape route to higher places.

begriffe.erklaerung: Japanese for harbour wave, a series of huge waves, usually after an undersea earthquake.
Earthquake whose centre lies below the seabed.
Network of measuring devices that warns of a danger before it arrives.
Place where one tectonic plate sinks beneath another.

gewusst: The highest tsunami wave ever observed was set off by a rockfall in Lituya Bay in Alaska in 1958 and surged more than 500 metres up a slope.
A tsunami can cross a whole ocean in less than a day.
The undersea earthquake of 2004 was so strong that it made the whole Earth vibrate slightly.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Stocker is a Swiss climate physicist at the University of Bern. He is one of the internationally known climate researchers and led part of the fifth world climate report.
wichtigste: Thomas Stocker was born on 1 July 1959.
He studied environmental physics at ETH Zurich.
From 1993 he led the Division of Climate and Environmental Physics in Bern.
From 2008 to 2015 he was co-chair of Working Group I of the IPCC.
In 2017 he received the Marcel Benoist Prize.
Among other things, he researched the bipolar seesaw.

abschnitte.text: **Thomas Stocker** was born on **1 July 1959**. He studied **environmental physics** at **ETH Zurich** and completed a doctorate in **1987**. After that he did research in London, Montreal and New York, among other places. In **1993** he became a professor at the Physics Institute of the **University of Bern**. There he led the Division of **Climate and Environmental Physics**, which is known for its work on **ice cores**.

abschnitte.titel: Work for the world climate council
abschnitte.text: The **IPCC**, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, sums up what is known about the climate in large reports. From **2008 to 2015** Stocker was **co-chair of Working Group I**, together with a Chinese colleague. This group deals with the scientific basis. Its report for the Fifth Assessment Report came out in **2013**. In 2015 the Federal Council nominated him to chair the IPCC. However, the South Korean economist **Hoesung Lee** was elected.

Stocker researched how the northern and southern hemispheres are connected. If the ocean current that brings warmth into the **North Atlantic** weakens, the north cools down. At the same time the south slowly warms up. This pattern is called the **bipolar seesaw**. Ice cores from **Greenland** and **Antarctica** show it.

In **2017** Stocker received the **Marcel Benoist Prize**. It is considered the most important science prize in Switzerland. In 2026 he received the **Alfred Wegener Medal** of the European Geosciences Union. It is named after the German polar researcher **Alfred Wegener**, who founded the theory of continental drift.

gewusst: Ice cores contain tiny trapped air bubbles that show what the air was made of hundreds of thousands of years ago.
When the IPCC report he co-led came out in 2013, Stocker was 54 years old.

teile.einleitung: A dripstone cave is a cave in which stone icicles grow from the ceiling and the floor. They form from limestone that the water brings with it and they grow very slowly. In Switzerland you can visit such caves, for example the Höllgrotten in the canton of Zug.
wichtigste: Dripstone caves usually form in limestone.
Water dissolves lime from the rock and deposits it again in the cave.
Dripstones grow very slowly, often only millimetres in many years.
In caves it is roughly equally cool and damp all year round.
The Höllgrotten near Baar are in the canton of Zug.
The Hölloch in the Muota Valley is one of the longest caves in the world.
You must not touch dripstones, because the grease from your skin disturbs their growth.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater takes up a little **carbon dioxide** in the soil and becomes slightly acidic. This lets it dissolve **lime** from the rock. When this water drips into a cave, it gives off part of the gas into the air. Then a tiny bit of lime is left behind. Drop by drop, a dripstone grows like this over a very long time.

Dripstones that hang down from the ceiling are called **stalactites**. The stones that grow upwards from the floor are called **stalagmites**. When the two meet, a **column** forms. A memory aid: stalactites hold on tight to the ceiling. Sometimes thin straws, curtains or small pools of lime also form.

The **Höllgrotten** lie near Baar in the canton of Zug and are open to visitors. There you can see many beautiful dripstones. The **Hölloch** in the Muota Valley in the canton of Schwyz is more than 200 kilometres long and is one of the longest caves in the world. It has been explored by **cavers** for many decades. They wear a helmet and a lamp and draw exact plans of the passages.

abschnitte.titel: Life and climate in the cave
abschnitte.text: Deep inside the mountain you notice little of the weather outside. That is why it is roughly **equally cool** in caves all year round. The air is usually damp. **Bats** like to hibernate in caves, because it is quiet, dark and frost-free there. Visitors should not disturb them.

If you visit a dripstone cave, take a **warm jacket** and sturdy shoes, even in summer. The ground can be wet and slippery. You must **not touch** the dripstones. The grease from your skin stays on the stone, and no new lime can be deposited there. That way the stones stay beautiful for everyone.

gewusst: A broken dripstone often needs thousands of years to grow as big again.
Because dripstones grow in layers, researchers can learn from them about the climate of earlier times.
